power.intro: Is each plant making what the grid asked for, how well does it use its fuel, and what's wearing it down?

dga.title: Transformer oil analysis
dga.intro: Faults inside a transformer break the oil down into gases. How much gas there is gives the condition (1 normal to 4 act now); which gases, plotted on the Duval triangle, say what kind of fault.
dga.triangleLabel: Duval triangle with each transformer's latest oil sample
dga.summaryAllNormal: All {{count}} transformers are condition 1 (normal). Their points sit where healthy oil usually does.
dga.tableCaption: Latest oil sample of each transformer
dga.conditionNote: Conditions follow IEEE C57.104 (2008): the worst single gas, or the total, sets it.
dga.gasesCaption: Dissolved gases in the latest sample, ppm

performance.none: No performance measures for this kind of equipment yet.
performance.washAdvice: Fouling has pushed this turbine past the wash trigger: plan an offline compressor water wash at the next low-demand window.
performance.eohIntro: Equivalent operating hours (EOH) count fired hours plus {{perStart}} for every start, because heating up and cooling down wear the hot parts too. The hot parts are inspected every {{interval}} EOH; every second inspection is a major overhaul.
performance.duvalLabel: Duval triangle with {{id}}'s last oil samples, joined oldest to newest
performance.duvalSummary: The last {{count}} samples, oldest to newest: from {{from}} to {{to}}.

solar.title: Solar operations
solar.intro: How much energy are we losing, and where? Each plant against what its sunlight should give.
solar.notInScope: That plant isn't in the area you've picked. Choose another plant or widen the area.
solar.noPlants: There are no solar plants in the area you've picked.
solar.powerIntro: Expected power comes from a model of the plant: the sunlight measured on the panels, their temperature, the dust on them, and the inverters' limit. The gap is energy lost to faults.
solar.powerLabel: Plant power and expected power over the last 48 hours, in MW
solar.powerSummary: Over the 48 hours the plant made {{pct}} % of what was expected. Peak {{peak}}, at {{when}}.
solar.lossesTitle: Where the energy went, last {{days}} days
solar.lossesIntro: From the sunlight that fell on the panels to what reached the grid, one loss at a time. The performance ratio is the last bar divided by the first.

waterfall.label: {{name}} energy losses over the last {{days}} days
waterfall.summary: Of {{sun}} the sunlight could have given, {{actual}} was delivered (performance ratio {{pr}} %). Biggest loss: {{biggest}}, {{biggestPct}} %.

solar.invertersIntro: Each tile is one inverter: the energy it made as a share of what the sunlight should have given it. Stronger shading means a bigger shortfall. Pick a tile for its details.
solar.stringsIntro: A string is a chain of panels. Strings on the same inverter see the same sun, so one making under {{pct}} % of its sisters' median has a problem: often a failed bypass diode or a hot spot.
solar.noStrings: Every string is keeping up with its sisters.
solar.cleaningIntro: Dust costs a little more every day; a wash costs the same each time. The cheapest rhythm balances the two.

advice.clean_now: Wash now: the dust now costs more than a wash
advice.wait: No wash needed yet: next in about {{days}} days

cleaning.how: Best interval = √(2 × wash cost ÷ (daily revenue × dust rate)), at {{price}} USD per MWh.

solar.bessIntro: Batteries charge from the panels at midday and give it back in the evening peak. Health is the capacity left compared with new; a growing spread between cell voltages means cells drifting apart.
solar.socLabel: Battery charge over the last 48 hours, in %
solar.socSummary: Charging through the middle of the day, emptying into the evening.

solarPerf.powerIntro: Expected is what the sunlight should have given this inverter. A steady gap whenever the sun is up often means the inverter is limiting itself, for example because its cooling is failing and it cuts power to protect itself.
solarPerf.powerLabel: {{id}} power and expected power over the last 48 hours, in MW
solarPerf.powerSummary: Made {{pct}} % of expected over the last 24 hours.
solarPerf.stringsIntro: Each string's energy over the last 24 hours as a share of its sisters' median.
solarPerf.stringPowerIntro: The dashed line is the median of the other strings on the same inverter: same sun, same temperature. A string that stays below it has a problem of its own.
solarPerf.stringPowerLabel: {{id}} power and its sister strings' median over the last 48 hours, in kW
solarPerf.stringPowerSummary: Made {{pct}} % of its sisters' median over the last 24 hours.
solarPerf.socLabel: {{id}} charge over the last 48 hours, in %

oilGas.title: Oil & gas operations
oilGas.intro: Wells, pipelines and the refinery: are we producing what the reservoir allows, is the steel thick enough, and what needs cleaning or inspecting?

partWhat.upstream: Getting oil and gas out of the ground: wells and their pumps
partWhat.midstream: Moving it: pipelines and compressor stations
partWhat.downstream: Processing it: refinery equipment and inspections

card.downstream: Exchangers, vessels, tanks and relief valves
card.segmentsFlagged_one: {{count}} segment with thin wall or poor protection
card.segmentsFlagged_other: {{count}} segments with thin wall or poor protection

up.declineIntro: As a reservoir empties, its pressure drops and wells make a little less every month. Fitting a curve to the history shows the trend and forecasts it; days below the curve are oil lost to something else, like a failed pump.
up.declineLabel: Daily oil rate over the last 180 days with the fitted decline curve and a 180-day forecast
up.fitSummary: Fitted decline: {{pct}} % a year (fit quality r² = {{r2}}, where 1 is perfect).
up.noFit: Not enough production to fit a decline curve.
up.espIntro: An ESP is a long electric pump down the well that lifts the oil. Its motor temperature, current and intake pressure tell what's wrong before it fails.
up.wellsIntro: Biggest losses first. Lost oil is what the well would make with its pump working as designed.

diagnosisMeans.normal: Temperature, current and intake pressure are where they should be.
diagnosisMeans.motor_hot: The motor winding is past its temperature alert, so its insulation is ageing fast. Usually: less fluid flowing past to cool it, or a failing motor. Reduce the drive frequency and plan a workover.
diagnosisMeans.low_intake: The pump is drawing the well down faster than the reservoir refills it (pumping off), or gas is getting in. Slow it down.
diagnosisMeans.high_amps: The motor is working harder than usual: wear, sand, or heavier fluid.
diagnosisMeans.stopped: The pump isn't running, so its well is shut in and making nothing.

mid.profileIntro: Measured by the latest in-line inspection. The dashed line is the minimum the pipe needs to hold its pressure safely ({{required}} mm, from Barlow's formula).
mid.profileLabel: Pipeline wall thickness by distance along the route, in mm
mid.segmentsIntro: Shortest remaining life first. Remaining life uses the worse of two corrosion rates: the long-term one (metal lost since new) and today's probe reading. Cathodic protection holds the pipe at a small negative voltage to stop it corroding; it should be at least −{{cp}} V.
mid.compressorsIntro: Compressors push the gas along. Efficiency below design wastes fuel; a small surge margin means the machine is close to surge, where gas flow reverses violently and can wreck it.

down.exchangersIntro: Deposits build up inside exchangers and insulate the tubes, so less heat gets through (and the furnace burns more fuel to make up). Effectiveness compares the heat transferred with a clean exchanger; plan a clean before it falls below {{clean}} %.
down.inspectionsIntro: Industry codes set how often steel that holds pressure or product must be inspected: at most a fixed number of years, and sooner when it's corroding fast (half its remaining life).
down.noneDue: Nothing is overdue or due in the next 90 days.

codeMeans.api_510: Pressure vessels: internal inspection at least every 10 years, or at half the remaining life if that's sooner.
codeMeans.api_653: Storage tanks: internal inspection at least every 20 years, or at half the remaining life if that's sooner.
codeMeans.api_576: Relief valves are bench-tested every 3 years in dirty or corrosive service, otherwise every 5, and sooner if they leak.
codeMeans.ili: Pipelines are inspected from the inside by a tool called a pig at least every 7 years, or at half the remaining life if that's sooner.

perf.wellDeclineIntro: This well declines about {{pct}} % a year. Days far below the curve point at its pump.
perf.wellDeclineLabel: {{id}} daily oil rate with its fitted decline curve and forecast
perf.effLabel: {{id}} effectiveness over the last 30 days, in %
perf.lifeHow: Remaining life = (measured − required) ÷ the worse of the two rates.

reliability.intro: How often does equipment fail, how long does it take to fix, and which failures and which assets cost the most? From five years of failures coded with ISO 14224.

kpi.mtbfHow: Operating hours ÷ failures, for all the assets together. Higher is better.
kpi.mttrHow: Average hands-on repair time per failure. Lower is better.
kpi.repeatsHow: The same failure again on the same asset within 90 days: often a sign the first repair didn't fix the real cause.

reliability.monthlyIntro: A rising trend is worth investigating before it shows in availability. The first and last months are only partly inside the period.
reliability.monthlySummary: {{total}} failures in the period; the busiest month had {{peak}}.
reliability.paretoIntro: A Pareto chart: failure modes from biggest to smallest, with the running total. Usually a few modes cause most of the trouble; fix those first.
reliability.paretoLabel: Failure modes ranked by {{by}}, share of the total and running total, in %
reliability.paretoSummary_one: {{count}} of {{total}} failure modes makes 80 % of the total: {{modes}}.
reliability.paretoSummary_other: {{count}} of {{total}} failure modes make 80 % of the total: {{modes}}.
reliability.classesIntro: Pick a type to focus the page on it. Failure rate is failures per asset per year, so big and small fleets compare fairly.
reliability.badIntro: Assets failing at least {{ratio}} times as often as the average of their type. A small number of bad actors often causes a large share of the work; each deserves a root-cause analysis.
reliability.noBad: No bad actors in the period.

failuresTab.compareIntro: Every {{name}} in the company over the same years, for comparison.
failuresTab.compareCaption: This asset's reliability measures beside its type's
failuresTab.startRca: Start a root-cause analysis for this asset
failuresTab.listCaption: Failures of this asset, newest first

weibull.title: Weibull analysis
weibull.intro: How does the chance of failure grow with running time, for one type of equipment and one way it fails? The answer decides whether replacing on a schedule helps.
weibull.data: Fitted from {{failures}} times between failures and {{suspensions}} items still running ("suspensions": we know they lasted at least that long).
weibull.tooFew: Too few failures of this mode to fit a curve (at least 5 are needed).

patternMeans.infant_mortality: Failures are most likely soon after a repair or installation, then less likely. Look at installation, commissioning and part quality. Replacing on a schedule would make things worse: every new part starts in its riskiest period.
patternMeans.random: Age doesn't matter: an old item is as likely to fail as a new one. Replacing on a schedule won't help; watch its condition instead, and fix it when the condition says so.
patternMeans.wear_out: The longer it runs, the likelier it fails. Replacing or overhauling on a schedule works: about {{b10}} days would keep failures to roughly 1 in 10. Condition monitoring can stretch that safely.

weibull.plotIntro: Each dot is a failure; up is the estimated share failed by that age. On this special paper a Weibull is a straight line, so dots close to the line mean the fit is good. A bend or two different slopes suggests two failure causes mixed together.
weibull.plotLabel: Weibull probability plot: running time in days on a log scale, share failed on a Weibull scale
weibull.plotSummary: {{n}} failures. Fitted line: β {{beta}}, η {{eta}} days.
weibull.curveTitle: Reliability: the chance of still running
weibull.curveIntro: R(t) is the chance an item survives to age t without this failure. The dashed lines are the 90 % band: with this much data, the true curve is very likely between them.
weibull.curveLabel: Reliability against running time in days, with its 90 % band
weibull.curveSummary: 10 % have failed by {{b10}} days (B10); the average life is {{mttf}} days.

risk.title: Risk matrix
risk.intro: Every asset placed by how likely it is to fail within a year and how bad that would be. Risk = likelihood × consequence; work on the top-right first.
risk.matrixIntro: {{total}} assets. Pick a cell to list its assets.
risk.caption: Number of assets in each cell of the risk matrix
risk.axes: Up: likelihood of failing within a year (from the asset's own failure history, or an open prediction if that says more). Across: consequence, the asset's criticality.
risk.itemsIntro: Each asset links to its failure history.
risk.itemsCaption: Assets with their likelihood, consequence and risk

fmea.title: FMEA
fmea.intro: Failure mode and effects analysis: each way a type of equipment fails, scored for how bad it is, how often it happens and how likely we are to catch it first. The product (RPN) shows where maintenance effort pays most.
fmea.tableIntro: Highest risk first. Act on anything with RPN {{rpn}} or more, and on any mode with severity {{severity}} or more whatever its RPN.
fmea.plan_one: {{count}} asset of this type; {{preventive}} preventive work orders open for them.
fmea.plan_other: {{count}} assets of this type; {{preventive}} preventive work orders open for them.
fmea.caption: Failure modes with severity, occurrence, detection, risk priority number and maintenance strategy
fmea.severityFull: Severity: how bad a failure would be (1–10)
fmea.occurrenceFull: Occurrence: how often it happens, from the failure history (1–10)
fmea.detectionFull: Detection: how hard it is to see coming (1 easy, 10 invisible)

strategyWhy.time_based: It wears out: replace or overhaul on a schedule, around B10 ({{b10}} days).
strategyWhy.condition_based: Watch its condition and act when it changes; a schedule wouldn't match how it fails.
strategyWhy.redesign: It fails early after repair or installation: a schedule would make it worse. Improve the part, the fitting or the checks.
strategyWhy.run_to_failure: Cheap and harmless when it fails: let it, and fix it then.

fmea.scales: S, O and D are each 1 to 10, so RPN runs from 1 to 1,000. Detection is lower (better) where a predictive model already watches for the mode.

rca.intro: Investigations into why something failed, so it doesn't happen again: the timeline, 5 Whys, a fishbone of possible causes, the root cause, and corrective actions that become work orders.
rca.newIntro: Bad actors and repeat failures are the best candidates.
rca.timelineIntro: The asset's failures, work orders and predictions around the problem.
rca.whysIntro: Start from what happened and ask "why?" until the answer is something you can fix. Five is a rule of thumb, not a law.
rca.fishboneIntro: Also called an Ishikawa diagram: the problem at the head, and six places causes usually hide. List everything plausible first, then test them.

categoryHint.machine: The equipment itself, its parts and tools
categoryHint.method: Procedures, work instructions, the PM plan
categoryHint.measurement: Readings, instruments, what we didn't measure
categoryHint.environment: Weather, heat, dust, the site around it

rca.rootLabel: The root cause, in a sentence
rca.rootHint: Needed before the investigation can be closed.
rca.actionsIntro: What will stop it happening again. Each action can raise a work order straight away.

vibration.neverRunning: This machine hasn't been running when a measurement was due in the last 12 weeks, so there are no spectra to show.
vibration.orders: BPFO {{bpfo}}×, BPFI {{bpfi}}×, BSF {{bsf}}×, FTF {{ftf}}× running speed
vibration.journalNote: No defect frequencies; proximity probes show the shaft's orbit instead
vibration.noFindings: No fault patterns found: mostly running speed (1×), as in a healthy machine.

bearing_outer_race.title: Rolling bearing, outer-race defect
bearing_outer_race.why: A peak at the outer-race frequency (BPFO, {{hz}} Hz, {{amp}}). Every ball strikes the damaged spot as it passes. Plan a bearing change; the waterfall shows how fast it's growing.

bearing_inner_race.title: Rolling bearing, inner-race defect
bearing_inner_race.why: A peak at the inner-race frequency (BPFI, {{hz}} Hz, {{amp}}) with sidebands one running speed either side, because the damage turns with the shaft. Plan a bearing change.

oil_whirl.title: Oil whirl in a journal bearing
oil_whirl.why: A peak just under half running speed ({{hz}} Hz, {{amp}}): the oil film is dragging the shaft round instead of holding it. Usually wear or too little load on the bearing; check clearance and oil.

flow_instability.title: Flow instability
flow_instability.why: Broad energy well below running speed ({{amp}} in total): the flow through the machine is breaking up, as it does close to surge or at very low flow. Check the operating point and the anti-surge control.

misalignment.title: Misalignment
misalignment.why: The 2× peak ({{hz}} Hz, {{amp}}) is about as big as 1×. Shafts that aren't in line flex twice a turn. Check the coupling alignment at the next stop.

unbalance.title: Unbalance
unbalance.why: Nearly all the vibration is at running speed ({{hz}} Hz, {{amp}}) and the level is past alert. A heavy spot goes round once a turn. Balance the rotor.

vibration.spectrumIntro: How much the machine shakes at each frequency. Dashed lines mark where each kind of fault would show. Arrow keys move the cursor.
vibration.spectrumLabel: Vibration spectrum of {{point}} on {{date}}, amplitude against frequency
vibration.spectrumSummary: The largest peak is {{amp}} at {{hz}} Hz ({{order}}× running speed).
vibration.waterfallIntro: One spectrum a week, newest in front. A peak that grows week by week rises out of the floor like a ridge. The highlighted one is the spectrum above.
vibration.waterfallLabel: Weekly vibration spectra of {{point}}, {{n}} measurements, newest in front
vibration.orbitIntro: The path of the shaft centre over a few turns, {{date}}, from two probes at right angles. An ellipse is normal; loops inside it mean something slower than the shaft. The dots mark each turn.
vibration.orbitSummary: {{x}} µm across horizontally and {{y}} µm vertically, peak to peak.
vibration.noOrbit: No orbit for this machine: it runs on rolling bearings, which don't have proximity probes. Its bearing defects show in the spectrum instead.

twin.intro: Every asset in one area of a site, laid out the way the area works, with its health and values. Replay any hour of the last three days to see what happened when.
twin.activity_one: Something in this area was past a limit in {{count}} of the last {{hours}} hours.
twin.activity_other: Something in this area was past a limit in {{count}} of the last {{hours}} hours.
twin.stripLegend: In the strip, grey is normal; the colours mark the worst level that hour (alert, alarm, trip).
twin.legend: Border colour and word show health; a warning sign says which sensor is past which limit.
twin.tabIntro: Where {{id}} sits in its area, right now (outlined).
twin.replayLink: Replay the last three days in the digital twin
twin.invertersLabel: Inverters in {{name}}, each with its strings
twin.stringsNote: Each string shows its performance index: its output against its sister strings (100% = as good as the others).

pm.intro: Preventive maintenance plans, built from FMEA: a planned replacement for each failure mode that wears out, a regular condition check for each one a measurement can catch early. PM compliance is the share done on time.

kpi.complianceHow: PMs due in the last {{days}} days that were done within their window (a week, or a tenth of the interval if longer)
kpi.overdueHow: Past their window, not done, and no work order raised yet

pm.monthlyIntro: Each month: the share of PMs due that month that were done on time, against the target.
pm.monthlyLabel: PM compliance by month, last 12 months
pm.monthlySummary: {{pct}} over the last 90 days, against a target of {{target}} %.
pm.plansIntro: Most overdue first. Open a plan to see every machine it covers and raise the work that's due.
pm.plansCaption: PM plans with their interval, the assets they cover, compliance and what's due
pm.uncoveredIntro: FMEA recommends no preventive work for these: either it's cheaper to fix them when they fail, or the right answer is to change the design or how it's installed.

why.time_based: {{mode}} wears out with age, so it's replaced on a schedule, before about 10 % would have failed (B10 life about {{b10}} days).
why.condition_based: {{mode}} can be seen coming, so it's checked regularly and fixed only when a check finds something.

planned_remedy.1: Isolate and lock out the machine under a permit to work.
planned_remedy.3: Check alignment, leaks and that it runs as it should.
planned_remedy.4: Return it to service and record the readings.

condition_check.1: Take the readings on the route (vibration, temperature, a look and a listen).
condition_check.3: Raise a work order if anything is out of range.

pm.generateHelp: For every machine overdue or due in the next {{days}} days that has no work order from this plan yet. They arrive in the plan, ready to schedule.
pm.planMonthlyLabel: PMs due each month for plan {{id}}, last 12 months
pm.planMonthlySummary: {{pct}} done on time over the last 90 days.
pm.assetsIntro: Overdue first, then by next due date.
pm.assetsCaption: Assets covered by this plan, with their PM status

inventory.intro: Spare parts at every site: what's on the shelf, what's on its way, and what PM plans and failure predictions will need in the next {{days}} days. Parts that will run short come first.

kpi.shortHow: Needed before a new order could arrive, and not enough on the shelf or on its way
kpi.reorderHow: On hand plus on order is at or below the reorder point: time to order

inventory.linesIntro: One part at one site. Reorder point / max: order when stock on hand and on order falls to the first number, back up to the second.
inventory.linesCaption: Stock lines with status, stock, reorder levels, demand and what to order
inventory.noPmPlan: None: used only when a failure needs it
inventory.demandTitle: Who needs it in the next {{days}} days
inventory.demandIntro: PM replacements coming due, and failures that open predictions expect by their median remaining life.
inventory.woIntro: What this work will use, and whether the site has it.
inventory.woIssued: Taken out of stock when the work was closed out.
inventory.woNotEnough: Not enough on the shelf: order before scheduling.

hse.intro: Is anything safety-critical at risk? Safety-critical equipment and what's impairing it, permits waiting to be issued, incidents and changes under review.

kpi.impairedHow: Impaired: health warning or critical, a PM overdue, or an active P1 alarm
kpi.tierHow: Process safety events (losses of containment) by consequence, as in API RP 754: tier 1 the more serious

hse.monthlyTitle: Process safety events and near misses
hse.monthlyIntro: Columns: losses of containment each month (tier 1 and 2). Line: near misses reported. Many near misses for each event is a healthy sign: warnings heard early.
hse.monthlyLabel: Process safety events and near misses by month, last 12 months
hse.monthlySummary: {{tier1}} tier 1 and {{tier2}} tier 2 events, {{nearMisses}} near misses in the last 12 months.
hse.scesIntro: Relief valves, vessels, pipelines, tanks, separators, fired heaters, and any equipment of the highest criticality.
hse.scesCaption: Safety-critical equipment with its health and what impairs it
hse.permitsIntro: Hazardous work needs a permit to work, raised when it's scheduled. Work can't start until the HSE officer issues it; it closes when the work is closed out.
hse.permitsCaption: Permits to work with their work order, asset, planned start and status
hse.cannotStart: Work can't start until this permit is issued.
hse.incidentsIntro: The last 12 months. Process safety events come from the failure history (a leak of process fluid is a loss of containment); anyone on site can report a near miss.
hse.reportIntro: Something that could have hurt someone or damaged something, but didn't. Reporting it is how the next one is prevented.
hse.mocIntro: Before plant, a setting or a procedure changes, the change is written down, its risk assessed, reviewed and approved. Many major accidents started with a change nobody reviewed.

esg.intro: Greenhouse-gas emissions over the last {{days}} days, worked out from the plant's own measurements: fuel burned, gas flared and methane released. Each site against this year's target, and the part poor equipment health adds.

kpi.co2eHow: Combustion + flaring + methane, in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent
kpi.methaneHow: Vented and leaked gas: compressor seals, pipelines, gas-driven valves, wellheads, flare slip. Counted ×{{gwp}} as CO₂-equivalent (IPCC AR6, 100 years).
kpi.avoidedHow: Solar output × the grid's emission factor: what the grid didn't have to burn
kpi.avoidableHow: What poor equipment health added: fouled turbines burning more fuel per MWh, leaking pipelines, gas flared while compressors were down

esg.dailyTitle: Emitted and avoided, day by day
esg.dailyIntro: Emissions dip when plants turn down and rise on hot days, when turbines need more fuel for each MWh.
esg.dailyLabel: Tonnes of CO₂e emitted and avoided each day, last {{days}} days
esg.dailySummary: Combustion {{combustion}} t, flaring {{flaring}} t, methane {{methane}} t CO₂e; solar avoided {{avoided}} t.
esg.sitesIntro: Intensity is emissions for what a site produces: tonnes per MWh for power, kilograms per barrel of oil equivalent for oil and gas.
esg.sitesCaption: Sites with emissions, methane share, intensity, progress against target and emissions avoided
esg.emittersIntro: The 20 assets emitting most. Avoidable is what their condition adds: fixing it cuts emissions and cost together.
esg.emittersCaption: The assets emitting most, with source, emissions, avoidable part and health

reason.downtime: {{value}} t: flared while compressors were down

financials.intro: What maintenance cost over the last 12 months, and what predictions saved. Every figure shows how it was worked out.

kpi.valueHow: Failures prevented {{avoided}} − what the jobs cost {{cost}}
kpi.atRiskHow: Each open prediction's probability × what its failure would cost (repair and lost production)
kpi.downtimeHow: Hours each failure stopped production × what an hour of lost production costs that business
kpi.spendHow: Labour at {{rate}} an hour plus parts at stores prices
kpi.plannedHow: Preventive and predictive work as a share of spend. Planned work costs far less than repairing failures.

financials.monthlyTitle: Spend each month against the budget
financials.monthlyIntro: Corrective repairs, PM and predictive jobs together. The line is the budget, spread evenly over the year.
financials.monthlyLabel: Maintenance spend each month, last 12 months
financials.monthlyOver: Spent {{total}} against a budget of {{budget}}: {{difference}} over.
financials.monthlyUnder: Spent {{total}} against a budget of {{budget}}: {{difference}} under.
financials.kindsIntro: A repair after a failure costs many times a planned job.
financials.kindsCaption: Maintenance spend by kind of work, last 12 months
financials.downtimeIntro: An hour lost at an oil and gas site costs far more than an hour at a solar park.
financials.downtimeCaption: Hours lost to failures and what they cost, by site, last 12 months
financials.valueIntro_one: The most valuable jobs. Value = the failure prevented − labour at {{rate}} an hour − parts. {{count}} job found nothing wrong (a false alarm), so it prevented nothing and counts only as cost.
financials.valueIntro_other: The most valuable jobs. Value = the failure prevented − labour at {{rate}} an hour − parts. {{count}} jobs found nothing wrong (false alarms), so they prevented nothing and count only as cost.
financials.valueCaption: Finished predictive jobs, with what each prevented and cost
financials.noValue: No predictive jobs finished in the last 12 months.

reports.intro: Ready-made reports, a shift handover and a builder for your own. Every report prints, or saves as a PDF from the print dialog.
reports.reportIntro: Print it, or choose "Save as PDF" in the print dialog. The report covers the scope chosen at the top of the page.
reports.buildIntro: Pick the sections you need. The report below updates as you go, and the page's address remembers your choice, so you can bookmark it or send it as a link.
reports.handoverDescription: This shift so far, urgent alarms still open, work in progress and notes for the next crew.
reports.buildDescription: Choose your own sections from everything the reports can show.
reports.buildLink: Tip: copy the page's address to share this report or open it again later.
reports.noSections: Choose at least one section above.
reports.figuresCaption: {{title}}: each figure and how it was worked out

weekly-reliability.title: Weekly reliability report
weekly-reliability.description: Key measures, the top risks, failures over the last year, PM compliance and the alarm load.

monthly-esg.title: Monthly ESG report
monthly-esg.description: Emissions, intensity and targets per site, with safety alongside.

monthly-financials.title: Monthly financial report
monthly-financials.description: Value from predictions, cost of downtime, spend against budget, PM and spare parts.

management-summary.title: Management summary
management-summary.description: One report for the leadership meeting: measures, risks, money, emissions and safety.

risks.title: Top risks
risks.intro: The assets most likely to fail soon, weighted by what a failure would cost.

rel.failuresHow: Across {{assets}} assets, from the failure history
rel.availabilityHow: Share of hours the equipment could run
rel.repeatsHow: The same mode again on the same asset within 90 days

pm.complianceHow: PM jobs done within their window, last 90 days
pm.overdueHow: Past their window, not done and with no work order yet

alarms.intro: ISA-18.2 sets the targets: about 1 alarm per 10 minutes per operator, and a flood is more than 10.
alarms.totalHow: Every time an alarm sounded, repeats included

inv.shortHow: Fewer in stock than the demand forecast needs
inv.reorderHow: At or below the reorder point

hse.impairedHow: Safety-critical equipment whose health is warning or worse
hse.tierHow: API RP 754 tiers, by the size of the release

handover.intro: What the next shift needs to know. Print it for the handover meeting, or leave a note below.
handover.title: {{shift}} shift handover, {{from}}–{{to}}
handover.utc: Shifts run 06:00–18:00 and 18:00–06:00 UTC. Times are in UTC.
handover.alarmsIntro: P1 and P2 alarms that are still active, most urgent first.
handover.eventsIntro: The events that matter most this shift, most serious first.
handover.notesIntro: From this shift and the one before, newest first.
handover.addNote: Leave a note for the next shift (all sites)
handover.addNoteSite: Leave a note for the next shift about {{site}}
handover.noteAdded: Note left for the next shift

data.intro: Where the data comes from, and whether it can be trusted. Every prediction is only as good as the readings under it.
data.tagsIntro: Every measured signal (tag) with its limits, latest reading and any data-quality issue.
data.sourcesIntro: The systems feeding the platform. In this demo they're simulated, but their figures come from the plant's own data.

kpi.completenessHow: Share of expected readings that arrived: one per tag every {{minutes}} minutes, last {{hours}} hours
kpi.gapsOrBadHow: Tags with at least {{threshold}} % of readings missing or flagged bad. The odd dropped reading is normal; more is a problem.

issueHow.no_data: Tags that sent nothing in 24 hours: the asset is offline, or its link to the plant is down
issueHow.flatline: Tags reading exactly the same value for hours: a stuck sensor or transmitter. A frozen reading looks healthy, which is what makes it dangerous.

data.worstIntro: No data first, then stuck sensors, then bad quality and gaps; most affected first.
data.tagsCaption: Tags with their asset, latest reading, quality, limits and any data-quality issue

admin.intro: Who can do what, and who changed what. The platform's own health at a glance.

kpi.sourcesHow: Plant historian, CMMS, lab, ERP and weather; see Data & Integrations
kpi.completenessHow: Share of expected readings that arrived, whole enterprise, last 24 hours
kpi.changesHow: Every change made through the system, from the audit log

admin.limitsWhere: Alarm and trip limits are edited where they're shown:
admin.recentIntro: The latest entries in the audit log.
admin.noChanges: No changes yet in this session. Acknowledge an alarm, raise a work order or edit a limit, and it appears here.

users.intro: Everyone who uses the platform, and their role. A role decides which pages someone sees and what they can do.
users.caption: People, their role, job title and sites

roles.intro: What each role can open and do. Pages a role can't use are hidden from its menu, and show "no access" if opened by address.
roles.modulesIntro: Use: full access. View: can look but not change. No: hidden.

hierarchy.intro: The enterprise as the platform sees it: regions, sites, areas and equipment. Open a level to load the next.

audit.intro: Every change made through the system: who, when, what and to which item. Written by the server, so nothing can be left out.
audit.caption: The audit log: when, who, what, which item and what changed

limits.title: Limits for {{tag}}
limits.description: {{what}}. Alarms use the new limits from their next check, including for faults already developing.
limits.hint: Leave a box empty to remove that limit. Each limit must be above the one before it, from low trip to high trip.
limits.order: Limits must rise from low trip to high trip, each above the one before.

models.intro: The models behind the predictions: one per kind of equipment. How each version scored on past failures, what technicians found when they checked its predictions, and new versions waiting to be approved.
models.candidatesIntro: Each candidate was retrained on more data and scored on past failures. Retrained isn't always better: compare it with the version in production before approving.
models.candidatesCaption: Candidate model versions compared with production
models.awaiting: Waiting for a reliability engineer or analyst
models.allIntro: Backtest: precision (of the failures it predicted, how many really happened), recall (of the failures that happened, how many it predicted in time) and median warning. Live: technicians' verdicts on its predictions, last 12 months; under {{min}} verdicts is too few to judge.
models.allCaption: Models in production with backtest, live verdicts and open predictions

rules.intro: Simple threshold rules: "if this signal goes above a value for so many minutes, raise an alert". Test a rule on the last {{hours}} hours of real readings before saving it.
rules.listIntro: How often each rule would have fired in the last {{hours}} hours.
rules.demoNote: In this demo, rules are tested on recorded readings; they don't raise live alarms.
rules.buildIntro: Pick a kind of equipment and one of its signals, then a threshold and how long it must last. A spell shorter than that is ignored, which stops a single noisy reading raising an alert. Test it on the last {{hours}} hours to see how often it would fire.
rules.result_one: Would have fired {{count}} time, on {{assets}} of {{checked}} assets, in the last {{hours}} hours.
rules.result_other: Would have fired {{count}} times, on {{assets}} of {{checked}} assets, in the last {{hours}} hours.
rules.name: Rule name
rules.testFirst: Test the rule first: changing any value needs a new test.

whatIf.intro: What if we wait? Pick a predicted failure and how long the repair is put off, and see the chance the failure comes first and what that's worth.
whatIf.none: No open predictions with a remaining-life estimate.
whatIf.chanceHow: From the prediction's remaining-life estimate, given it hasn't failed yet
whatIf.expectedHow: Chance × failure cost ({{failure}}) + (1 − chance) × repair cost
whatIf.extraHow: Chance × (failure cost − repair cost): what the wait is likely to cost
whatIf.curveTitle: Chance the failure comes before the repair
whatIf.curveIntro: Remaining life: 10 % chance by {{p10}} days, 50 % by {{p50}}, 90 % by {{p90}} from the estimate, {{elapsed}} days ago. Lives are skewed (a long tail of late failures), so the curve is a log-normal fitted through those points.
whatIf.curveLabel: Chance {{asset}} fails before a repair on each date, next 90 days
whatIf.curveSummary: Chance of failing first if the repair waits 30 days: {{d30}}; 60 days: {{d60}}; 90 days: {{d90}}.
